TRANQUILLITATIS · PROCELLARUM
SIX DAYS OF THE MOON · APOLLO PASSIVE SEISMIC EXPERIMENT · 1969–1975

TRANQUILLITATIS · PROCELLARUM

APOLLO LUNAR MUSIFICATION · A MOONWORK BY SHOOK (D.V. ROGERS) · ALLSHOOKUP.ORG

WHAT YOU ARE HEARING

Six days of ground motion recorded by the Apollo Passive Seismic Experiment: the vertical mid-period channel (MHZ) of station S11 at Tranquility Base (Mare Tranquillitatis) and station S12 in the Ocean of Storms (Oceanus Procellarum). The raw MiniSEED day-files from the 2022 re-archive are bundled inside this page and decoded in your browser. No server, no external code.

The Moon's seismic signature is slowness. The crust is bone-dry and shattered by four billion years of impacts, so energy scatters rather than dissipates. Events build for minutes and ring for an hour. The work keeps that slowness with two clocks. A pitch clock (default 960×) sets where the waveform sits in the audible band. At 960× the seismometer's own 2.2 s pendulum resonance sounds at about 436 Hz, close to A4, so the instrument supplies the tonal centre. A separate structure clock sets how fast you travel through the day. It races through quiet hours and slows to as little as 24× when the Moon is moving.

THE SIX MOVEMENTS

#DAY-FILEWHAT IS IN THE RECORD
I · ARRIVALS11 · 21 Jul 1969 · peakedThe record opens at 07:03 UTC, after the moonwalk, so there are no footfalls. Several hours of heavy disturbance follow while the crew are aboard Eagle. The 17:54 UTC liftoff falls inside a telemetry gap (17:05–18:08) and is not in the record. The data resume with a slow drift and instrument re-centring.
II · QUIETS11 · 26 Jul 1969 · peakedMid lunar day: sparse short local events and one emergent event, with a ten-hour telemetry gap (08:29–18:40) that passes as a brief loss of signal.
III · HEATS11 · 2 Aug 1969 · peakedLate in the first lunar day: local cracks and pops before the station's night shutdown. (Most thermal moonquakes appear on the short-period sensor, so here the crystal voice is an interpretation driven by impulsiveness and temperature drift.)
IV · THE BELLS12 · 20 Nov 1969 · peakedCrew on the surface (EVA-2, about 03:55–07:44 UTC). Then the discarded ascent stage of LM Intrepid strikes the surface about 76 km away at 22:17:17.7 UTC: an emergent swell peaking at about 22:22 and still ringing near 23:10. This was the first seismic source on another world with a known time and place.
V · FRACTURES12 · 13 Mar 1973 · peaked (partial day, ends 14:21)A large shallow moonquake: first arrivals at about 08:01:30 UTC, peak energy 08:05–08:15, and a coda that rings for roughly three hours.
VI · EARTH CALLINGS12 · 7 Mar 1975 · flat modeNo moonquake. The instrument is in flat mode (15 s natural period, no pendulum peak, so the bell becomes a bar). The day is dominated by Earth-commanded pulse trains (09:11–10:20 and about 13:20). To verify against the pdart command log: calibration or re-levelling.

VOICES

True voice: direct audification at the pitch clock, granular so it can be time-stretched. Coda cloud: grains scattered across the surrounding minute of data, so you hear the scattering itself. Its brightness follows the lunar thermometer, the seismometer's rest position drifting with surface temperature. Bell / bar: resonators tuned to the instrument's own physics, excited by onsets: a 2.2 s pendulum bell in peaked mode, a 15 s free bar in flat mode (folded up by octaves where needed). Seismic FM: ground velocity drives the modulation index. Sub bed: the energy envelope on the pendulum fundamental. Found telemetry: everything usually filtered away, including saturation slabs, re-levelling steps, calibration ringing, the 10-bit staircase, a tick at every 54.34 s telemetry block (90 frames), clicks at gap edges, and a hiss of lost signal when a long gap is skipped. Thermal crystals: short grains triggered by impulsive moments. Light delay: an "Earth" copy of the true voice arrives late by the 1.28 s Moon–Earth light time, scaled by the structure clock.

HONESTY NOTES

The Moon is the composer and the algorithms are translators. Real high-frequency content above 3.3 Hz (the MHZ Nyquist) is not in these files, so any brilliance above the pendulum band is synthesis driven by real low-band features. S11 and S12 never recorded at the same time: S11 fell silent in August 1969, before S12 began in November. Event times and labels here come from inspecting the waveforms. Classifications marked "local, unclassified" have not been checked against the Nakamura catalog. Artefacts are not deleted: they are masked out of the true voice and routed to the telemetry bus, and they are shown in brown on the dial. Timestamps are Earth-reception times (they include the 1.2–1.4 s light delay), and the sampler clock drifted with lunar temperature. The archive's timing trace (ATT) is not bundled, so that drift is not used here.

THE MOON IS STILL ONLY HEARD THROUGH APOLLO

NASA switched the Apollo network off on 30 September 1977. Its successor, the Farside Seismic Suite (JPL, with seismometers inherited from Mars InSight), is built, tested and flight-ready. In July 2026 NASA and Draper ended the CP-12 task order that was to carry it to Schrödinger basin, after delays pushed the landing to 2030 or later. These recordings remain the only multi-year, multi-station seismic record of the Moon.

LINEAGE

Sounds of Seismic → SE1STR0N1CA → S3D → ELYSIUM MARS MUSIFICATION → TRANQUILLITATIS · PROCELLARUM. A single HTML file with zero dependencies: an ES5 main thread, an AudioWorklet engine and seeded randomness (SEISMETA). Each movement is deterministic for a given start point.
